Constraints: Limited public information on Hellberg Safety’s current consumer reach and sales channels.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Need to rely solely on publicly available sources; financial data may not be accessible.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand or willingness to pay for a differentiated offering.. T1: Consumers will adopt hearing protection as a fashion or lifestyle accessory if it is styled, marketed as personal expression, and sold through channels that emphasize aesthetics and social sharing, leading to multiple purchases per user and premium pricing. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety gains higher margins through design-led premium pricing and increased unit volume from repeat purchases.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as a visible accessory that signals status or personal style, they will purchase multiple pairs for different contexts (e.g., work, leisure, fashion) rather than a single utilitarian item.. How value is captured: By controlling design, branding, and retail channels, Hellberg can charge premium prices and capture value through accessories and limited editions.. Assumptions: Consumers currently see hearing protection as purely functional and are price-sensitive.; There is an unmet demand for stylish, customizable ear protection in consumer markets.; Marketing can shift perception from safety tool to lifestyle product.. Predictions: In a test offering a limited-edition, fashion-forward earplug, purchase intent will exceed that of a standard industrial model.; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for the fashion version than for the standard version.; Average revenue per user will be above the current price point for standard earplugs..

T2: Consumers will adopt hearing protection as a health and wellness product if it is marketed as part of a broader lifestyle of ear health, comfort, and active living, leading to higher adoption among non-industrial users. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety gains market expansion into consumer segments and can command premium pricing for health-focused features.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view hearing protection as essential for maintaining hearing health and enjoying outdoor activities without discomfort, they will purchase it proactively rather than reactively.. How value is captured: By integrating health messaging, comfort features, and wellness branding, Hellberg can differentiate its products and capture value through higher-margin consumer lines.. Assumptions: Consumers currently prioritize hearing protection for industrial safety and are unaware of its role in personal health.; There is a growing consumer interest in hearing health and active lifestyles.; Marketing can position earplugs as a wellness accessory rather than just safety gear.. Predictions: In a test offering a health-focused earplug with comfort features, purchase intent will exceed that of a standard industrial model.; Users will report higher perceived health benefits and willingness to pay a premium.; Repeat purchase rate will be driven by health maintenance rather than single-use scenarios..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Fashion vs Health Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase intent.. Sample: 500 adult consumers (ages 18-45) recruited via panel, balanced for gender and geographic region (Sweden, Germany, UK).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each concept.. Predictions: T1: Fashion concept will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than health concept.; T2: Health concept will achieve higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than fashion concept.. Decision rule: If fashion concept purchase intent >= 35% and health concept purchase intent < 30%, proceed with fashion-focused differentiated proposition. If health concept purchase intent >= 35% and fashion concept purchase intent < 30%, proceed with health-focused differentiated proposition. If neither meets 35% threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay for a fashion‑focused versus a health‑focused differentiated proposition. If the fashion concept meets the 35% purchase intent threshold and outperforms the health concept, proceed with a fashion‑led differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain the current B2B/industrial focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households with small gardens will adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales in the growing consumer market and leveraging existing dealer network.. Why behaviour changes: Rapidly increasing demand for garden tractors as households find them practical and economical, as evidenced by market growth and competitor success.. How value is captured: Deere can sell lawn tractors through its existing dealer network, capturing value from premium pricing and brand association with quality.. Assumptions: Demand for garden tractors continues to grow in the 1960s.; Deere can adapt its tractor engineering to produce a consumer-friendly lawn tractor.; Deere dealers will promote and sell the new consumer product.. Predictions: If Deere launches a lawn tractor, sales will increase proportionally to the growth rate of garden tractor demand.; Deere's market share in the lawn tractor segment will rise relative to competitors like Wheel Horse..

T2: Deere will launch a lawn tractor because its existing dealer network already sells garden tractors, creating a ready distribution channel and brand exposure that reduces market entry risk. Who benefits: Deere benefits by leveraging its established dealer relationships to introduce a new consumer product without building a separate sales force.. Why behaviour changes: Dealers are already selling garden tractors (including competitor brands) because Deere did not offer one, indicating existing consumer demand and dealer willingness to promote garden equipment.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling lawn tractors through the same dealer network, using existing relationships to reach consumers and maintain brand consistency.. Assumptions: Dealers will continue to promote garden tractors even after Deere introduces its own brand.; Deere can adapt its tractor engineering to meet consumer lawn tractor specifications.; The dealer network is willing to allocate shelf space and marketing effort to a new Deere lawn tractor.. Predictions: If Deere launches a lawn tractor, dealer sales activity for garden tractors will increase, and Deere's market share will grow relative to competitors.; Dealers will report higher customer interest in Deere lawn tractors compared to other brands, due to brand familiarity from existing Deere farm equipment..

Test "Dealer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Survey a sample of John Deere dealers about their willingness to promote a new Deere lawn tractor versus a competitor brand, and measure their expected sales impact.. Sample: 50 John Deere dealers in regions with known garden tractor demand (identified from market data).. Measure: 1) Percentage of dealers who would allocate shelf space and marketing effort to a Deere lawn tractor. 2) Estimated increase in garden tractor sales (units) if Deere launches a lawn tractor.. Predictions: T1: Dealers will show low willingness to promote Deere lawn tractors because demand is driven by consumer need for inexpensive, practical equipment, not by dealer relationships.; T2: Dealers will show high willingness to promote Deere lawn tractors because they already sell garden tractors and have existing consumer demand, making entry low risk.. Decision rule: If ≥60% of surveyed dealers indicate they would allocate shelf space and marketing to a Deere lawn tractor, and the estimated sales increase is ≥10% of current garden tractor sales, proceed with development. Otherwise, do not invest.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden households, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network. The evidence shows strong, rapid demand for inexpensive, practical garden tractors (76% sales growth, Wheel Horse demand) and that Deere already built a prototype and evaluated competitors, indicating technical feasibility. The dealer network already sells garden tractors, Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, dealer willingness, or Deere's engineering capabilities for lawn tractors. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden households, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network. The evidence shows strong, rapid demand for inexpensive, practical garden tractors (76% sales growth, Wheel Horse demand) and that Deere already built a prototype and evaluated competitors, indicating technical feasibility. The dealer network already sells garden tractors, Target customer: Households with small gardens seeking inexpensive, practical lawn equipment.. Value proposition: A Deere lawn tractor that combines farm‑tractor reliability with consumer‑friendly features, sold through existing dealers to capture premium pricing and brand association.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Dealer Preference Test (50 dealers, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to promote a Deere lawn tractor and estimated sales impact. If the test meets the decision threshold (≥60% dealer willingness and ≥10% sales lift. Uncertainty: Dealer willingness to prioritize a Deere brand over competitors; the extent to which existing garden‑tractor sales will translate to Deere sales; and whether the prototype can meet consumer expectations for simplicity and cost.. Would change if: If the Dealer Preference Test shows <60% dealer willingness or <10% sales lift, indicating the dealer network is not a viable entry point.; If new evidence shows that consumer demand is driven by brand reputation rather than price/practicality, weakening T1.; If a competitor launches a significantly cheaper lawn tractor, altering the market dynamics.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Dealer Incentive Test for Lawn Tractor Introduction" between T1; T2. Method: Randomly assign Deere dealers to two groups: Group A receives a standard incentive (e.g., a modest rebate on farm-tractor sales) to stock a new lawn tractor; Group B receives a higher incentive (e.g., a larger rebate plus promotional support) to stock the same lawn tractor. Both groups are offered the same product specifications derived from Deere’s existing tractor engineering. Track the number of lawn tractors sold by each group over 12 weeks.. Sample: 50 Deere dealers with existing farm-tractor sales in regions where garden tractor demand is known to be growing (based on pre-1962 market data).. Measure: Number of lawn tractors sold by each group during the 12‑week period.. Predictions: T1: Sales will be driven by consumer demand for inexpensive, practical garden tractors; the incentive level will have little effect on total sales because demand is already high.; T2: Sales will be driven by dealer motivation; the higher incentive group will sell significantly more lawn tractors than the standard incentive group.. Decision rule: If the higher‑incentive group sells at least 20% more lawn tractors than the standard‑incentive group, proceed with a full dealer rollout using the higher incentive structure. If the difference is less than 10%, conclude that consumer demand (T1) is the primary driver and consider a lower‑cost entry. If the difference is between 10% and 20%, conduct a follow‑up test with a different incentive type.. Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product for outdoor recreation if it offers active listening features (e.g., Bluetooth, FM radio) that preserve sound quality while protecting hearing, because they value both safety and enjoyment during activities. Who benefits: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, cyclists, dog walkers) who need hearing protection but also want to hear surroundings or music.. Why behaviour changes: Current hearing protectors block all sound, limiting enjoyment. Active listening models reduce this barrier, making protection feel less restrictive and more convenient for recreational use.. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium price for integrated audio features and sell through specialty outdoor retailers or direct-to-consumer channels, capturing higher margins than basic earplugs.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participants are willing to pay more for hearing protection that does not isolate sound.; Active listening technology is reliable and comfortable for extended outdoor use.; Hellberg can design and manufacture such products within its existing capabilities.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation users will indicate intent to purchase a hearing protector with active listening at a price 20% above standard models.; Sales of a differentiated outdoor-recreation line will exceed 5% of total consumer sales within 12 months if marketed appropriately..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product for home office or remote work if it offers comfort and discreet design that allows prolonged wear without fatigue, because they need protection during long work hours without sacrificing productivity. Who benefits: Remote workers, home office professionals, and freelancers who spend many hours in noisy home environments.. Why behaviour changes: Standard earplugs can be uncomfortable for extended wear, leading users to skip protection. A comfortable, discreet design reduces fatigue and encourages consistent use, making protection feel like a productivity enhancer rather than a hind. How value is captured: Hellberg can position the product as a premium ergonomic solution, sell through office supply retailers or direct-to-consumer, and capture higher margins by emphasizing comfort and brand reputation for quality.. Assumptions: Remote workers are willing to pay a premium for hearing protection that is comfortable for 8+ hour days.; Comfortable earplugs do not significantly impair speech understanding or communication.; Hellberg can design and produce ergonomic earplugs within its existing manufacturing capabilities.. Predictions: Surveyed remote workers will indicate intent to purchase a comfortable, discreet hearing protector at a price 15% above standard models.; Sales of a differentiated home-office line will represent at least 3% of total consumer sales within 12 months if marketed to remote work segments..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical vs Fitness Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either medical necessity framing (disease prevention) or fitness tracking framing (weight loss/progress). Participants indicate purchase intent at a fixed price point (e.g., $120) and willingness to pay a premium over a basic scale.. Sample: 400 adults recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported health/fitness engagement. Randomly assigned 200 to medical framing, 200 to fitness framing.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness to pay (continuous). Secondary: self-reported health concern and fitness goal intensity.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the medical framing group compared to fitness framing.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the fitness framing group compared to medical framing.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between groups is at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 55% vs 45%) and the 95% confidence interval for the difference does not include zero, proceed to develop the framing that shows higher intent. If the difference is below 10 percentage points or not statistically significant, conclude insufficient evidence to justify a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Commercial Marine PLB Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 outdoor recreationists (verified via self-reported activity in past 12 months) and 250 commercial marine operators (verified via vessel ownership or industry affiliation).. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary ("Would you buy a PLB for your use case?") 2) WTP: maximum amount willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Outdoor recreationists will show purchase intent >=60% and WTP >=€500; commercial marine operators will show purchase intent <30% and WTP <€300.; T2: Commercial marine operators will show purchase intent >=60% and WTP >=€500; outdoor recreationists will show purchase intent <30% and WTP <€300.. Decision rule: If outdoor recreationists meet T1 purchase intent and WTP thresholds AND commercial marine operators meet T2 thresholds, proceed with consumer proposition. If only one group meets its thresholds, prioritize that segment. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreationists, leveraging the 406 MHz PLB as a safety necessity. Begin with a limited retail launch in high-participation regions (e.g., Alaska, Pacific Northwest) at the suggested $700 price point, while continuing B2B operations. Use the proposed survey test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for outdoor recreationists, leveraging the 406 MHz PLB as a safety necessity. Begin with a limited retail launch in high-participation regions (e.g., Alaska, Pacific Northwest) at the suggested $700 price point, while continuing B2B operations. Use the proposed survey test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, campers, scouts) who engage in remote activities and view PLBs as insurance-like safety equipment.. Value proposition: A PLB that provides reliable satellite distress alerting in remote environments, marketed as essential safety gear comparable to insurance, with retail pricing around $700 and availability through outdoor retailers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Commercial Marine PLB Purchase Intent Test (500 participants, €15,000, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for outdoor recreationists versus commercial marine operators.. Uncertainty: Actual consumer demand and willingness to pay are unknown; the test will determine if purchase intent and WTP meet thresholds. Regulatory mandates for commercial marine are also uncertain and would require separate evidence.. Would change if: If the test shows outdoor recreationists fail to meet purchase intent >=60% or WTP >=€500, or if commercial marine operators meet T2 thresholds, the recommendation would shift to prioritize that segment or reject expansion.; If new evidence shows strong regulatory mandates for commercial marine PLBs or high adoption rates among marine operators, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would change.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

Test "Outdoor Recreation vs Home Office Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 self-identified outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, cycling, camping) and 250 remote workers/home office users.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary choice ("Would you buy this product?") 2) WTP premium: percentage above a baseline price of $30 (e.g., "How much more would you pay for a product with [feature]?" 3) Conversion simulation: if offered at baseline price, would they purchase? (binary).. Predictions: T1: Outdoor recreation group will show purchase intent >=60% and WTP premium >=20% for a comfort/style-focused product; remote workers will show purchase intent <40% and WTP premium <10%.; T2: Remote workers will show purchase intent >=60% and WTP premium >=15% for an active-listening product; outdoor recreation group will show purchase intent <40% and WTP premium <10%.. Decision rule: If outdoor recreation group meets both purchase intent >=60% and WTP premium >=20% thresholds, proceed with outdoor recreation differentiated proposition. If remote workers meet both purchase intent >=60% and WTP premium >=15% thresholds, proceed with home office differentiated proposition. If neither group meets its thresholds, recommend no expansion. If both groups meet thresholds, prioritize the group with higher combined WTP premium.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Outdoor Recreation vs Home Office Preference Test (10 weeks, €15,000) to gather direct consumer evidence before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical Necessity vs. Fashion Appeal" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and fitness interest. Randomly assigned to either medical necessity framing (n=250) or fashion/status framing (n=250).. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary "Would you buy a home BIA device priced at €150?" 2) Maximum WTP: open-ended numeric response. 3) Secondary: self-reported importance of health monitoring vs. style.. Predictions: T1: Medical framing will yield higher purchase intent and WTP than fashion framing.; T2: Fashion framing will yield higher purchase intent and WTP than medical framing.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for medical framing exceeds fashion framing by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed with medical-necessity consumer proposition. If fashion framing exceeds medical framing by at least 10 percentage points, proceed with fashion-oriented proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health-conscious consumers who view body-fat measurement as a medical necessity for disease prevention. Value proposition: A branded, medically validated home body-fat analyser positioned as a preventive health tool, sold through trusted retail channels, with optional data-tracking services.. Use the 10-percentage-point decision rule to decide.. Uncertainty: Actual consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home BIA device are unknown; the test will determine whether the medical-necessity framing generates sufficient purchase intent to justify investment.. Would change if: If the test shows fashion framing outperforming medical framing by ≥10 percentage points, we would reconsider a fashion-oriented proposition.; If purchase intent for medical framing is below 30% or the difference between framings is <10 percentage points, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B markets.. Why behaviour changes: Home office workers currently either remove hearing protection to communicate or use generic earplugs that block sound; a product that enables clear audio while protecting hearing removes this trade-off, encouraging adoption.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through higher-margin direct-to-consumer sales and cross-selling of accessories (e.g., charging cases, ear tips) to a growing remote-work segment.. Assumptions: Remote work and home office adoption are sustained at levels that generate significant demand for hearing protection.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for active listening capabilities in hearing protectors.; Hellberg can integrate Bluetooth/FM technology into a comfortable, discreet earplug design.. Predictions: Surveyed home office workers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% more for a hearing protector with active listening features.; Pilot sales of a differentiated home office earplug will achieve a conversion rate of at least 4% among target users within 12 weeks..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Outdoor Recreation vs Home Office Hearing Protection" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product purchase. Participants are randomly assigned to either an outdoor recreation earplug (emphasizing comfort, style, and discreet design) or a home office earplug (emphasizing active listening features like Bluetooth/FM radio). They are shown product images, descriptions, and a price point (premium over standard earplugs by 20% for outdoor and 15% for home office). They indicate whether they would purchase and at what price. The test also collects demographic data to segment results.. Sample: 500 participants recruited via an online panel, balanced between outdoor recreation enthusiasts (250) and home office workers (250).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. Secondary measure: perceived importance of comfort/style vs active listening features.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor recreation group will show purchase intent >=5% and WTP at least 20% above standard earplug price.; T2: Home office group will show purchase intent >=4% and WTP at least 15% above standard earplug price.. Decision rule: If outdoor recreation group meets its purchase intent threshold (>=5%) and home office group does not (or vice versa), the corresponding theory is favoured. If both meet thresholds, both theories remain plausible. If neither meets thresholds, both are unlikely.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 400 respondents: 200 homeowners (DIY) and 200 boat owners, recruited via panel in Scandinavia and UK.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each product variant.. Predictions: T1: The durability‑focused variant (5‑year warranty, total cost of ownership messaging) will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and a willingness to pay premium of €10‑15 over the standard product.; T2: The safety‑focused variant (safety certification badge, expert endorsement) will achieve at least 10% higher purchase intent and a willingness to pay premium of €8‑12 over the standard product.. Test "Outdoor Recreation Hearing Protection Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown a product description for a differentiated hearing protection earplug designed for outdoor recreation (e.g., hunting, hiking). The description varies between two versions: Version A emphasizes safety and essential protection for the activity; Version B emphasizes integrated features such as Bluetooth connectivity and FM radio for music/communication. Participants are asked: "Would you purchase this product?" (Yes/No) and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open numeric field).. Sample: 300 adult outdoor recreation participants (hunters, hikers, fishermen) recruited via outdoor recreation forums and social media. Stratified to include both safety-focused and feature-focused interests.. Measure: Purchase intent (Yes/No) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) amount. Secondary measure: stated importance of safety vs. convenience features (1-5 scale).. Predictions: T1: Version A will generate a higher purchase intent rate and a WTP at least 20% above the baseline price of €35 (i.e., ≥€42).; T2: Version B will generate a higher purchase intent rate and a WTP at least 15% above the baseline price of €35 (i.e., ≥€40).. Decision rule: If Version A achieves purchase intent ≥45% and WTP ≥€42, proceed with safety-focused differentiated proposition. If Version B achieves purchase intent ≥45% and WTP ≥€40, proceed with integrated-features proposition. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion. If both meet thresholds, prioritize the version with higher WTP.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Outdoor Recreation Hearing Protection Preference Test (X1) to gather direct consumer evidence on willingness to pay for safety-focused versus integrated-features propositions. If the test meets the decision thresholds (purchase intent ≥45% and WTP ≥€42 for safety version or ≥€40 for integrated version), proceed with the corresponding 12‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Households with small gardens will adopt lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing premium pricing and brand loyalty from consumers seeking reliable garden equipment.. Why behaviour changes: Rapidly increasing demand for garden tractors (as evidenced by Wheel Horse's market success) indicates households view them as essential tools for small‑garden maintenance, prompting purchase decisions.. How value is captured: Deere can sell differentiated models through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering reputation to command higher margins than generic competitors.. Assumptions: The demand observed for Wheel Horse tractors reflects a broader consumer trend applicable to Deere's engineering capabilities.; Deere's dealer network can effectively reach individual consumers without major restructuring.; Consumers will associate Deere's brand with quality garden equipment, justifying premium pricing.. Predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated lawn tractor, sales will increase proportionally to the size of the small‑garden household segment.; Consumer surveys will show that price, practicality, and maintenance cost are primary purchase drivers.; Deere's market share in the lawn‑tractor segment will rise relative to competitors lacking a differentiated offering..

T2: Deere's existing dealer network and brand reputation will drive consumer adoption of lawn tractors, even without a differentiated product, because consumers trust Deere for quality and rely on dealers for service. Who benefits: Deere benefits by leveraging its established distribution to sell lawn tractors at standard margins, capturing value through brand trust and service contracts.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers historically purchase farm equipment through Deere dealers; they extend this trust to garden equipment, assuming reliability and after‑sales support.. How value is captured: Deere can sell lawn tractors through the same dealer network, using existing relationships to reach consumers without new marketing, and capture value through service and parts sales.. Assumptions: Deere's dealer network is capable of selling non‑farm equipment without major changes.; Consumers associate Deere's farm‑tractor reputation with garden equipment quality.; Service and parts revenue from lawn tractors will offset any lower unit margins.. Predictions: If Deere offers a non‑differentiated lawn tractor through dealers, sales will be driven by dealer activity rather than product features.; Consumer surveys will show brand trust as a primary purchase factor for garden equipment.; Deere's market share will increase in the lawn‑tractor segment even without product differentiation..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Marine vs Exterior Coatings" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 leisure yacht owners (recruited via marine forums) and 250 homeowners (recruited via home improvement sites).. Measure: 1) Choice: which product they would purchase (Jotun marine antifouling vs Jotun exterior paint). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for each product. 3) Brand association: self-reported perception of marine-grade durability.. Predictions: T1: Yacht owners will choose Jotun marine antifouling over exterior paint and indicate a WTP premium of at least 15% over generic marine brands.; T2: Homeowners will choose Jotun exterior paint over marine antifouling and indicate a WTP premium of at least 15% over generic exterior brands.. Decision rule: If yacht owners’ WTP premium ≥ 15% and homeowners’ WTP premium ≤ 10%, proceed with marine consumer proposition (supports T1). If homeowners’ WTP premium ≥ 15% and yacht owners’ WTP premium ≤ 10%, proceed with exterior consumer proposition (supports T2). If neither meets its threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Who benefits: Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand differentiation; consumers gain a product that fits their lifestyle while protecting hearing.. Why behaviour changes: Shift from viewing hearing protection as purely functional/industrial to a desirable accessory that signals personal care and outdoor readiness.. How value is captured: Higher price points, direct-to-consumer sales, and brand loyalty through lifestyle positioning.. Assumptions: Consumers in target segments (e.g., outdoor enthusiasts) currently purchase generic hearing protection or none.; They value comfort, aesthetics, and brand image as much as protection.; Hellberg can design a product that meets these lifestyle criteria while maintaining safety standards.. Why behaviour changes: Shift from generic or unbranded protection to a product endorsed by industry expertise and recognized certifications, reducing perceived risk.. How value is captured: Higher price justified by safety certification, brand reputation, and perceived reliability; potential for B2B2C partnerships.. Assumptions: Consumers research safety certifications before purchasing hearing protection.; Hellberg’s existing industrial reputation transfers to consumer perception.; Certifications (e.g., ISO, ANSI) are visible and trusted by target consumers.. Test "Lifestyle vs Certification Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) elicitation.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor forums) and 150 general consumers (recruited via consumer panels). Randomly assign each respondent to one of two between‑subjects conditions.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) for a hearing protector described with either lifestyle branding (colorful design, outdoor adventure imagery, "Peace of Mind" messaging) or safety certification branding (ISO/ANSI badges, "professional-grade safety", "certified by industry experts"). Secondary measure: purchase intent (binary: "Would buy").. Predictions: T1: Outdoor enthusiasts will show a WTP premium of at least 20% for the lifestyle‑branded version compared to the certification‑branded version.; T2: General consumers will show a WTP premium of at least 15% for the certification‑branded version compared to the lifestyle‑branded version.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for lifestyle branding among outdoor enthusiasts exceeds that for certification branding by ≥ 20%, proceed with lifestyle‑focused consumer proposition. If the average WTP for certification branding among general consumers exceeds that for lifestyle branding by ≥ 15%, proceed with certification‑focused proposition. If neither threshold is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Lifestyle vs Certification Messaging Test (X1) to obtain empirical evidence on willingness to pay for lifestyle branding versus safety certification. T1 revised: Simulated evidence SYN-A shows that styled protectors were worn no more often than plain ones, contradicting the assumption that lifestyle branding increases adoption. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product for a specific use case if they perceive it as a lifestyle accessory that enhances safety without compromising comfort or style, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases, provided the product is perceived as functional and not merely decorative.. Evidence: SYN-A.

Conduct the proposed Lifestyle vs Certification Messaging Test (X1) to obtain empirical evidence on willingness to pay for lifestyle branding versus safety certification. If the test meets its decision thresholds, proceed with the corresponding proposition; otherwise, maintain the current B2B/industrial focus. Target customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (e.g., hikers, cyclists) and general consumers seeking reliable hearing protection.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing protector that either (a) blends lifestyle aesthetics with proven safety performance for outdoor activities, or (b) emphasizes professional-grade safety certifications to build trust and justify premium pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 online conjoint survey (X1) with 300 respondents, measuring willingness to pay for lifestyle‑branded versus certification‑branded products.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because no public source directly demonstrates consumer willingness to pay for either lifestyle branding or safety certification. T1: Households with small gardens will purchase lawn tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for multiple chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Households with small gardens (consumer demand) and John Deere (through sales of lawn tractors and attachments).. Why behaviour changes: The market for garden tractors is growing as households adopt them for convenience and cost‑effectiveness, as evidenced by a 76% rise in lawn and garden equipment sales and the rapid demand for garden tractors described in contemporary news. How value is captured: John Deere can sell lawn tractors and attachments through its existing dealer network, capturing margin on each unit and building brand loyalty among consumers who value reliability.. Assumptions: Demand for garden tractors is driven primarily by cost, practicality, and ease of maintenance rather than brand prestige.; John Deere can leverage its existing dealer network to reach individual consumers without major infrastructure changes.; Consumers will prefer a brand they already trust for farm equipment when choosing a lawn tractor.. Predictions: If introduced, a differentiated lawn tractor would achieve a market share comparable to or greater than existing garden tractor brands within 12 months of launch.; Sales would be positively correlated with the price of competing garden tractors; a 10% price increase for a competitor would increase Deere’s units sold by at least 5%.; Dealer participation in selling lawn tractors would increase as they receive higher margin per unit compared to current garden tractor sales..

T2: Consumers will purchase lawn tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a modern convenience, leading to multiple purchases and brand loyalty, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Consumers seeking status and convenience (demand) and John Deere (through premium pricing and repeat purchases).. Why behaviour changes: The cultural shift in the early 1960s toward suburban homeownership and modern leisure activities makes lawn care a visible activity; owning a branded lawn tractor signals affluence and modernity, as suggested by the 76% sales rise and the . How value is captured: John Deere can capture value by positioning lawn tractors as premium, brand‑associated products, selling higher‑margin models and encouraging multiple purchases (e.g., different colors, attachments) through its dealer network.. Assumptions: Consumers associate brand reputation with quality and status in leisure equipment.; The suburban housing boom of the early 1960s creates a large base of households with small gardens seeking modern conveniences.; Deere’s existing dealer network can be leveraged to promote brand prestige without major changes.. Predictions: If introduced as a premium, branded lawn tractor, sales would be less sensitive to price than competing generic models, with a 10% price increase causing less than 5% drop in units sold.; Consumers would be willing to purchase multiple lawn tractors (e.g., for different garden areas) within 12 months, increasing average revenue per household.; Dealer participation would be driven by higher margin per unit and the ability to showcase brand prestige, leading to increased promotional activity..

Test "Price Sensitivity vs Brand Prestige Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two experimental groups of prospective consumers who have small gardens and are considering a lawn tractor. Both groups receive product information about a Deere lawn tractor (engineered from farm tractor technology) and its features. Group A receives a price discount of 15% off the standard retail price; Group B receives the same discount but is additionally told that the Deere brand is recognized for quality and status in modern leisure equipment, and that owners often purchase multiple tractors for different garden areas.. Sample: 200 individuals recruited via local gardening clubs and community boards in mid‑1962, stratified by age and household income to match suburban homeownership demographics. Randomly assigned 100 to Group A and 100 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent measured by willingness to pay (WTP) in euros for the discounted price and willingness to purchase a second unit within 12 months. Secondary measure: actual purchase behavior if a limited production run of 200 units is made available at the discounted price for 8 weeks.. Predictions: T1: Group A (price discount only) will show a WTP at least 10% higher than Group B, and overall purchase intent will be driven primarily by price reduction.; T2: Group B (price discount + brand prestige messaging) will show a WTP at least 10% higher than Group A, and overall purchase intent will be driven primarily by brand prestige and status messaging.. Decision rule: If Group A’s WTP ≥ 10% higher than Group B, proceed with a price‑focused rollout (supporting T1). If Group B’s WTP ≥ 10% higher than Group A, proceed with a prestige‑focused rollout (supporting T2). If the difference is less than 5%, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden households, leveraging existing tractor engineering and dealer network, but first validate demand through a price‑sensitivity test before full rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand drivers for lawn tractors. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden households, leveraging existing tractor engineering and dealer network, but first validate demand through a price‑sensitivity test before full rollout. Target customer: Households with small gardens in suburban areas (early‑1960s demographic).. Value proposition: A reliable, economical lawn tractor built on Deere’s farm‑tractor engineering, sold through existing dealers at competitive pricing, offering multiple attachments for varied garden tasks.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Price Sensitivity vs Brand Prestige Test (200 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent under price discount versus price discount plus prestige messaging.. Uncertainty: The extent to which consumers will prioritize price over brand prestige, and whether the prestige message can generate sufficient demand to justify a premium positioning.. Would change if: If the test shows Group B’s willingness to pay is at least 10% higher than Group A, indicating brand prestige drives demand, the recommendation would shift toward a prestige‑focused rollout (supporting T2).; If the test is inconclusive (difference <5%), further evidence or a larger test would be needed before committing.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical vs Fitness Framing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Predictions: T1: Medical framing group will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than fitness framing group.; T2: Fitness framing group will show higher purchase intent and higher WTP than medical framing group.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between groups is at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 55% vs 45%) and the average WTP difference is at least €20, proceed to develop the framing that yields higher intent. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home fitness, weight‑loss tracking) with a new marketing and distribution strategy.; 2) Expand the existing clinic/health‑club model into new B2B segments (e.g., gyms, corporate wellness programs) without creating a consumer brand.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on commercial scales and existing B2B body‑fat analyser distribution.; 4) License the technology to third‑party consumer brands or partners to reach individual buyers without direct consumer marketing..

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a medical necessity for disease prevention, leading to multiple purchases and willingness to pay a premium. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking health monitoring; Tanita benefits from premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of the link between excess body fat and chronic diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) creates a perceived need for accurate home measurement.. How value is captured: Tanita can charge higher prices for a consumer model, sell multiple units per household, and leverage its professional credibility to justify premium.. Assumptions: Consumers trust medical evidence and will act on it.; Home measurement accuracy is sufficient for personal health decisions.; Marketing can effectively communicate the medical necessity.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home model priced at 2-3x the professional unit.; Purchase intent will correlate with self-reported health concerns.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a model marketed as medically validated..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they view it as a fashion accessory or status symbol, leading to multiple purchases and willingness to pay a premium. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking self‑presentation and social signaling; Tanita benefits from premium pricing and brand extension into lifestyle.. Why behaviour changes: Rising consumer culture in the 1990s treats health‑related gadgets as visible markers of personal care and modernity, creating demand for distinctive, brand‑associated devices.. How value is captured: Tanita can price the consumer model as a lifestyle product, sell multiple units per household for different aesthetics, and leverage its professional credibility to justify premium.. Assumptions: Consumers associate health monitoring devices with personal style.; Brand recognition (e.g., "Tanita") adds perceived value beyond functionality.; Marketing can position the device as a fashionable accessory.. Predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate intent to purchase a home model priced at 2‑3x the professional unit when presented as a fashion item.; Purchase intent will correlate with self‑reported interest in health‑fashion or status goods.; Willingness to pay will be higher for a model marketed with lifestyle imagery and limited editions..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical Necessity vs. Fashion Positioning" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and health consciousness.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this device?") 2) Maximum price willing to pay (continuous, in euros).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP when exposed to medical necessity messaging compared to fashion messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP when exposed to fashion messaging compared to medical necessity messaging.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the medical messaging condition exceeds the average WTP for the fashion messaging condition by at least €50 (10% of a €500 price point), we conclude T1 is better supported. If the fashion condition exceeds the medical condition by at least €50, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than €50, we conclude insufficient evidence to favor either theory.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious consumers who view body‑fat measurement as a medical necessity, using Tanita’s professional credibility to justify premium pricing. Begin with a limited launch in health‑focused retail channels and gather consumer feedback before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health‑conscious consumers who view body‑fat measurement as a medical necessity, using Tanita’s professional credibility to justify premium pricing. Begin with a limited launch in health‑focused retail channels and gather consumer feedback before broader rollout. Target customer: Health‑conscious adults (ages 25–55) who are aware of the link between excess body fat and chronic disease and seek accurate home monitoring.. Value proposition: A home body‑fat analyser marketed as a medically validated tool for disease prevention, leveraging Tanita’s professional reputation to command premium pricing and multiple household purchases.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (500 US adults, randomized medical vs. fashion messaging, willingness‑to‑pay measurement) to validate demand and price tolerance before full launch.. Uncertainty: Actual consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home model; competitive landscape in 1993; accuracy concerns for home use; potential for fashion positioning to emerge.. Would change if: If the test shows fashion messaging yields higher willingness to pay by €50 or more, or if survey data reveals strong intent to purchase a fashion‑positioned device.; If new evidence shows a large existing consumer market for home body‑fat analyzers or a clear price ceiling below premium levels.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: unlikely.

Test "Residential Boat Paint Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) elicitation.. Sample: 500 Norwegian boat owners (DIY/homeowners) recruited via boat clubs and online panels, balanced for boat ownership duration and age.. Measure: 1) Choice: which paint brand they would purchase (Jotun marine vs generic marine). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for Jotun marine paint (in euros). 3) Stated importance of brand trust vs safety certification.. Predictions: T1: Higher choice share for Jotun when framed as "proven marine brand" and WTP at least 15% above generic price.; T2: Higher choice share for Jotun when framed as "safety-critical, corrosion protection" and WTP at least 20% above generic price.. Decision rule: If Jotun choice share > 45% and WTP premium >= 15% (for T1) OR > 45% and WTP premium >= 20% (for T2), proceed to develop differentiated consumer proposition. If neither threshold met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Residential Boat Paint Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare brand trust versus safety framing. If the test meets the decision thresholds (choice share >45% and WTP premium >=15% for T1, or >=20% for T2), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, recommend no expansion. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Residential Boat Paint Choice Test (X1) to empirically compare brand trust versus safety framing. If the test meets the decision thresholds (choice share >45% and WTP premium >=15% for T1, or >=20% for T2), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, recommend no expansion. Target customer: Norwegian boat owners who maintain their own vessels (DIY/homeowners).. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition leveraging Jotun’s marine expertise, offering proven antifouling performance and safety certification for residential boat maintenance, sold directly via Jotun’s website at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 10‑week, €15,000 choice‑based conjoint survey with 500 Norwegian boat owners.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on homeowner purchase behavior, willingness to pay, or brand trust. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows Jotun choice share below 45% or WTP premium below 15% (for T1) or 20% (for T2), we would recommend no expansion.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for safety‑certified marine paints or a clear brand‑trust premium, we would favor T2 and adjust the proposition accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Outdoor recreationists will adopt PLBs as a safety necessity, leading to multiple purchases per household and willingness to pay premium prices. Who benefits: ACR Electronics would benefit from higher-margin consumer sales and brand association with safety.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory mandate for PLBs in remote areas and public awareness of rescue success (e.g., Alaska rescues) create perceived necessity; insurance-like perception increases willingness to pay.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value through direct consumer sales at premium retail prices (e.g., $700) and potentially through accessories or service contracts.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates are sufficient to generate demand.; Consumers view PLBs as essential safety equipment, not optional.; ACR can reach consumers through retail channels and marketing.. Predictions: Households with outdoor recreation participants will purchase at least one PLB within 12 months.; Willingness to pay will be at least $500 for a PLB, with price sensitivity lower than for non-safety electronics..

T2: Insurance companies will subsidize PLBs for policyholders as a safety incentive, creating demand through bundled coverage rather than direct consumer purchase. Who benefits: ACR would benefit from volume sales and potential service contracts; insurers benefit from reduced claims and compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Insurers seek to lower risk exposure and meet regulatory expectations for safety equipment; offering PLBs as a bundled benefit makes it attractive to policyholders.. T1: Consumers will adopt Jotun’s marine‑grade protective coatings for residential boat maintenance because they trust the brand for durability and safety, and they value the convenience of buying directly online. Who benefits: Individual boat owners who need reliable antifouling and protective coatings for their vessels.. Why behaviour changes: Trust in Jotun’s marine expertise reduces perceived risk of product failure; direct‑to‑consumer online sales remove intermediary costs and provide immediate access, making the product attractive compared to competitors.. How value is captured: Jotun can charge a premium price for marine‑grade performance and capture margin on direct sales, while leveraging existing Multicolor distribution to reach consumers.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Jotun with high‑performance marine coatings.; Online purchase friction is low enough to drive adoption.; Competitors do not offer a comparable direct‑to‑consumer marine product.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for Jotun marine coatings sold directly online.; Sales of Jotun marine coatings through the consumer website will grow faster than overall marine segment sales.; Repeat purchase rate for boat owners will be higher than for general DIY customers..

T2: Consumers will adopt Jotun’s marine‑grade protective coatings for residential boat maintenance because they perceive a safety risk from inferior products and seek a trusted brand to mitigate that risk. Who benefits: Individual boat owners who prioritize safety and reliability for their vessels.. Why behaviour changes: Awareness of marine coating failures (e.g., corrosion, fouling) creates fear of product failure; Jotun’s reputation for marine expertise reassures consumers that the product will perform safely, prompting purchase.. How value is captured: Jotun can command a premium price for safety‑certified coatings and capture margin on direct sales, while leveraging existing brand trust to reduce marketing costs.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Jotun with proven marine safety performance.; Safety concerns outweigh price sensitivity for boat owners.; Competitors lack comparable safety certification or brand trust.. Predictions: Surveyed boat owners will rank safety as a top purchase criterion for marine coatings.; Willingness to pay a premium for Jotun will be higher when safety is highlighted.; Purchase intent will increase when Jotun is presented as the only safety‑certified option..

Test "Online Choice Experiment for Marine Coatings" between T1; T2. Method: Present participants with a simulated online purchase of Jotun marine antifouling coating. In one version, emphasize brand trust and convenience (direct online purchase, same-day delivery). In another version, emphasize safety certification and risk mitigation (safety label, warranty, expert endorsement). Measure willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent.. Sample: 300 individual boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media, balanced for age, gender, and boat ownership duration.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) and binary purchase intent (yes/no) for each version.. Predictions: T1: Higher WTP and purchase intent when convenience is highlighted, because trust and ease of purchase drive adoption.; T2: Higher WTP and purchase intent when safety is highlighted, because safety concerns outweigh convenience.. Decision rule: If average WTP for the convenience version exceeds the safety version by at least €15 (10% of a typical €150 price point), proceed with a convenience-focused consumer proposition. If the safety version exceeds the convenience version by at least €15, proceed with a safety-focused proposition. If the difference is less than €15, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed online choice experiment (Test X1) to measure willingness to pay for convenience versus safety messaging. If the convenience version yields at least €15 higher WTP, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition; otherwise, gather more evidence before deciding. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed online choice experiment (Test X1) to measure willingness to pay for convenience versus safety messaging. If the convenience version yields at least €15 higher WTP, proceed with a convenience-focused proposition; otherwise, gather more evidence before deciding. Target customer: Individual boat owners who need reliable antifouling and protective coatings for their vessels.. Value proposition: A direct-to-consumer online offering of Jotun marine-grade protective coatings, emphasizing brand trust and convenience (same-day delivery, easy purchase) to capture premium pricing and margin.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute Test X1 within the €20,000 budget and 12‑week timeline, using 300 boat owners recruited via marine forums and social media.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because no public source directly demonstrates consumer willingness to pay a premium for convenience or safety. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the convenience version shows at least €15 higher WTP than the safety version, we would proceed with a convenience-focused proposition.; If the safety version shows at least €15 higher WTP, we would pursue a safety‑certified proposition.; If the difference is less than €15, we would seek additional evidence before committing.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Lawn Tractor Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown a description of a John Deere lawn tractor (engineered from existing tractor technology) and asked to choose between two versions: a "Utility" version (emphasizing practicality, low cost, and suitability for small gardens) and a "Premium" version (emphasizing design, status, and leisure use). They also indicate willingness to pay a price premium (e.g., 10% above a baseline price).. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners with small gardens (self-identified) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and geographic region.. Measure: 1) Choice: which version selected. 2) Willingness to pay premium (percentage of participants willing to pay at least 10% more for the Premium version). 3) Self-reported importance of convenience vs. status.. Predictions: T1: Utility version will be chosen by at least 60% of participants, and willingness to pay a premium for the Premium version will be below 10%.; T2: Premium version will be chosen by at least 60% of participants, and willingness to pay a premium for the Premium version will be at least 10%.. Decision rule: If the Premium version is chosen by ≥60% of participants AND ≥10% of participants indicate willingness to pay a 10% price premium, then T2 is considered supported and a differentiated premium proposition is justified. If the Utility version is chosen by ≥60% and willingness to pay a premium is <10%, then T1 is supported and a cost‑focused proposition is justified. If neither condition is met, the test is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden homeowners, emphasizing practicality, low cost, and ease of use, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network. Begin with a limited launch of a utility‑focused lawn tractor model, using the €20,000 test budget to validate demand before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small‑garden homeowners, emphasizing practicality, low cost, and ease of use, leveraging Deere’s existing tractor engineering and dealer network. Begin with a limited launch of a utility‑focused lawn tractor model, using the €20,000 test budget to validate demand before broader rollout. Target customer: Homeowners with small gardens who need reliable, inexpensive yard‑work equipment.. Value proposition: A John Deere lawn tractor built from existing tractor engineering, positioned as a practical, economical tool for small‑garden maintenance, sold through the existing dealer network.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 10‑week, €15,000 consumer preference test to measure choice between utility and premium versions and willingness to pay a premium. If the test confirms demand for the utility version, proceed to a limited launch; otherwise,. Uncertainty: The extent to which affluent homeowners view lawn tractors as status symbols (T2) remains uncertain due to lack of direct evidence. The test will clarify whether a premium positioning is viable.. Would change if: If the test shows the Premium version is chosen by ≥60% of participants and ≥10% are willing to pay a 10% price premium, indicating status‑driven demand, the recommendation would shift toward a premium, design‑focused proposition.; If additional historical sources from 1962 reveal affluent suburban adoption or premium pricing strategies, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would adjust accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Hellberg Safety develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing hearing-protection offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Hellberg Safety should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hearing-protection offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited public information on Hellberg Safety’s current consumer reach and sales channels.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Need to rely solely on publicly available sources; financial data may not be accessible.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand or willingness to pay for a differentiated offering.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, industrial DIY, or home office) with unique features and branding.; 2) Expand the existing hearing‑protection line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., broader distribution, new packaging, or marketing to individual buyers).; 3) Maintain the current B2B/industrial focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).; 4) Pursue a different route to market for existing products (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce) without altering the product itself..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation) if it offers unique features that address their specific needs, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety would benefit from premium pricing and brand differentiation in a growing consumer segment.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers in outdoor recreation prioritize comfort, situational awareness, and durability; a product that meets these needs better than generic earplugs would be perceived as essential for their activities.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through higher price points, brand positioning as a specialist, and potential subscription or accessory sales.. Assumptions: There is measurable demand for hearing protection in outdoor recreation among individual consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for features that improve comfort and situational awareness.; Hellberg can design and manufacture a differentiated product within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget.. Predictions: If a test offers a differentiated outdoor-recreation earplug at a 20% price premium over standard earplugs, at least 30% of target consumers will purchase within 12 weeks.; Surveyed consumers will rate the differentiated product as “most suitable for their activity” at a higher frequency than standard earplugs..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection product for a specific use case if it is marketed as a lifestyle accessory that signals status and aligns with personal identity, leading to higher willingness to pay and brand loyalty. Who benefits: Hellberg Safety would benefit from premium pricing, brand elevation, and increased customer lifetime value through accessory sales.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers in lifestyle segments (e.g., music enthusiasts, outdoor adventurers) purchase products that reflect their identity and social standing; a hearing protector that looks distinctive and is marketed as part of a lifestyle would be. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through higher price points, limited-edition designs, and cross-selling of accessories (e.g., cases, ear tips) and brand collaborations.. Assumptions: There is a consumer segment that views hearing protection as a status symbol rather than purely functional.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for aesthetic differentiation and brand storytelling.; Hellberg can produce limited-edition designs within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget.. Predictions: If a test offers a lifestyle-branded earplug at a 20% price premium over standard earplugs, at least 25% of target consumers will purchase within 12 weeks.; Surveyed consumers will indicate they would recommend the product to peers for its style and brand association at a higher rate than standard earplugs..

Test "Use-Case vs Lifestyle Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) elicitation.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced between two segments: 200 self-identified outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, hunting, shooting) and 200 lifestyle consumers (music enthusiasts, fashion-conscious).. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary choice between a differentiated outdoor-recreation earplug (features: comfort, situational awareness, durability) and a standard earplug at a 20% price premium. 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for each product. 3) Secondary: open-ended reason for choice.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor-recreation segment will show purchase intent ≥30% and WTP at least 20% above standard earplug price; lifestyle segment will show purchase intent <20% and WTP at or below standard price.; T2: Lifestyle segment will show purchase intent ≥25% and WTP at least 20% above standard earplug price; outdoor-recreation segment will show purchase intent <20% and WTP at or below standard price.. Decision rule: If the outdoor-recreation segment meets T1 purchase intent threshold (≥30%) and the lifestyle segment meets T2 purchase intent threshold (≥25%), proceed to develop the corresponding differentiated proposition. If only one segment meets its threshold, prioritize that segment. If neither meets its threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Use-Case vs Lifestyle Preference Test (X1) to gather direct consumer evidence on willingness to pay and purchase intent for a differentiated outdoor-recreation earplug versus a standard earplug.  Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Use-Case vs Lifestyle Preference Test (X1) to gather direct consumer evidence on willingness to pay and purchase intent for a differentiated outdoor-recreation earplug versus a standard earplug. If the test confirms at least 30% purchase intent and a 20% price premium among outdoor-recreation enthusiasts, proceed to develop a use‑ Target customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hiking, hunting, shooting) who prioritize comfort, situational awareness, and durability in hearing protection.. Value proposition: A differentiated hearing-protection product tailored to outdoor recreation, featuring enhanced comfort, situational awareness, and durability, positioned as essential gear for their activities.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Use-Case vs Lifestyle Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €20,000 budget, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer evidence; the test will resolve this by providing purchase intent and WTP data for specific segments.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or no willingness to pay a premium for outdoor-recreation features, we would recommend no expansion.; If the lifestyle segment shows purchase intent above 25% and a premium, we would reconsider a lifestyle-focused proposition.; If new public sources reveal strong consumer demand for differentiated hearing protection in outdoor recreation, we would prioritize developing that proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
